preface: The Coalition Has Arrived and Nobody Approved My Throne
"My niggas," I announced, "tonight we make history."

"Tonight you make the table level," Rae said. She put one hand on the wobbling treaty desk and looked at the champagne balanced on its corner. History slid toward her wrist. She caught the glass without looking impressed.

I had advertised the evening as BUTCHES VERSUS STUDS: A NIGHT OF HIGH-STAKES DIPLOMACY. Six rooms of games. A coalition signing. A drag programme. A private casino floor and enough gold trim to make a reasonably secure country reconsider its reserves. The printer had asked whether versus meant a debate. I had said it meant ticket sales. There were no tickets. I was paying for everybody.

The first Great Butch vs. Stud War had happened in 1967 at the Blue Comet Social Club. That was the story I had been told. The story was entirely invented, and within that invention I had already managed to receive three incompatible versions. A borrowed jacket, a disputed jukebox selection and an unsigned peace agreement appeared in all three. The alleged artillery was a handbag full of coins.

Auntie June, eighty-two and still a butch with excellent posture, said she had won. Odessa, eighty-four, a stud everybody called Dez, said June had invented the rules after losing. They arrived in the same car. June carried Dez's bag. Dez was wearing a jacket that June recognised from 1967. I asked whether that was a provocation. "It's chilly," Dez said.
I had promised them a Second Great Butch vs. Stud War with a definitive ending. They had asked whether dinner was included. The veterans were already better at diplomacy than I was.

Kit arrived with a suit bag, a library tote and the posture of a woman who had already decided the sound system was inadequate. "I'm here for the karaoke," she said. Rae pointed at the crooked table. "I'm here because somebody said there would be decent food." I showed them their rival lecterns. They immediately used both to support the table.
"My niggas," Tank whispered, watching my international architecture become furniture repair, "peace is expensive."
"We haven't begun the rivalry."
"Your rivalry is holding up a buffet."

Nia came through the door carrying a fountain pen and wearing a dress that made Rae forget the table for just long enough to look up. Nia was a trans lesbian, a lawyer, and the first person to ask whether the signature page was attached to anything. I told her the lesbian delegation was on the left and the trans delegation was on the right. She looked between the doors.
"I already belong in both rooms. Are you charging me twice?"
"No."
"Good. Your borders are stupid."

She took two badges, clipped them together and sat beside Rae. Kit asked for a spare badge because hers would look good on her jacket. Within five minutes my factions had become accessories. I had spent four hundred dollars on velvet ropes to describe people who could simply walk around them.

Mika, the trans nonbinary planner, unhooked one rope and rolled it into a circle. They had a radio, three miniature model hotels in their bag, and a schedule that treated my welcome speech as a removable obstruction. "We're signing a game-night charter," they said. "Not dividing Europe. Move your face."

The face was mine, printed nine feet high on a backdrop. I had been photographed looking toward the future. The future needed the fire door behind me. Tank and Remy carried me sideways while I watched my own expression approach a mop cupboard.

Remy had come to perform as King Receipts. He was a trans man, a drag king, and the owner of a fanfare that began with an actual cash-register noise. Velvet Payroll heard the rehearsal through the wall and came over in a robe that had its own relationship with gravity. "Darling, if that sound means somebody's paying me, play it again."
"It's my entrance."
"Then enter with an invoice."

She wanted a full set, good light and a cheque that cleared. He wanted a microphone that worked and a partner who would stop laughing before the end of his love song. They settled the order of their first rehearsal by playing rock-paper-scissors. I had commissioned a twelve-page dispute mechanism. Nigga, they had used their hands for three seconds and gone back to work.
Shawna found me beside the unused lectern. "You look troubled."
"They're forming alliances without me."
"That's the event."

She kissed me, adjusted my collar and told me that if the signing finished before midnight, we could form a very private bilateral arrangement upstairs. I began caring about administrative efficiency with an intensity my accountant had never seen. I asked Mika whether the programme could be shortened. They handed me my own speech with every page crossed out.

Darnell arrived with the wrong jacket and a contribution nobody had put on the hospitality rider. "Who authorised cocaine at a coalition signing?" Velvet asked. "My fee doesn't include arguing with somebody who thinks his yacht is a personality."
"It's a beautiful yacht."
"Then marry it. The water's already booked."

Rosa pointed him away from the game table. Dre put his casserole in the space he vacated and claimed the blue controller. I started a sentence about Crip diplomacy. "Nigga, I brought dinner," he said. "Don't give the casserole a foreign policy."

Mercedes tried the microphone. Porsche checked the projector. Kit asked Rae whether she wanted to inspect the mystery games. Rae said yes, provided nobody made her sign an agreement to enjoy them. Nia held up the actual draft. "That clause is already gone."
"You read it?" I asked.
"I crossed out 'irrevocable fun.'"
"That was my best line."
"That's why I used the thick pen."

So here it is, Lillian: two hundred and forty games, six departments, and a summit full of grown people who can disagree about an entrance without surrendering a friendship. You can read the game cards, follow the ridiculous ceremony, enjoy the scenes or skip directly to a title that catches you. Nobody needs a coalition's permission to have a good evening.
I tried one final welcome. "My niggas, the treaty will bear witness to—"
"The table's level," Rae said.

Everyone applauded. Nia squeezed her hand. Kit turned on the karaoke screen. I had prepared a declaration of historic unity, and the first unanimous decision was that a woman fixing my furniture deserved the microphone more than I did.
Fair. Fucking humiliating. But fair.
Campaign Record: The First War, 1967
A fictional document from the equally fictional Blue Comet Social Club. This is invented family-and-club lore for the comedy, not an account of LGBTQ history.

June drove a bus, saved her tips from a second job, and bought a jacket with a lining she described as expensive. Dez made clothes and described the lining as polyester with ambition. Both remembered the jacket as magnificent. Each remembered being the reason it looked good.

On the night in question, June had put a coin in the jukebox. Dez had selected the record. June claimed ownership of the next dance by financial contribution. Dez claimed ownership by taste. The cashier claimed somebody still owed for two ginger ales. Every account omitted the ginger ales until the receipt turned up.

The first engagement occurred beside the coat rack. June asked where her jacket had gone. Dez said a jacket was only borrowed if the owner remembered lending it. June said that was the precise opposite of how borrowing worked. Dez said she looked good. June agreed, which has complicated every subsequent attempt to describe this as a clean military victory.

The second engagement involved the microphone. Neither woman had been scheduled to sing. Both later described the duet as an ambush. The club programme called it an unexpected highlight. A photograph shows them laughing so hard that the microphone has been pointed at a lampshade. June says this proves sabotage. Dez says the lampshade had a better sense of rhythm than the committee.

A peace agreement was drafted on the back of the hall-rental invoice. It provided for alternating jukebox selections, return of the jacket before winter and payment of the ginger ales. June signed the front. Dez signed the back. They put their names on opposite sides of the same obligation and each spent the next fifty-nine years saying the other had never signed.

No armies marched. The event was an extravagant name for a club feud, a dance, a little money and two people who liked having a reason to see each other again. Their friends called it a war because their friends were dramatic. I called the sequel a war because the banner company charged the same amount for any title under forty letters, and I had not counted.

Now the jacket was back in the room, the veterans were sharing a plate, and I had purchased a triumphal arch. June asked which side had won. I said the new coalition would settle the question. Dez looked at the arch. "Baby, the carpenter won."

The summit would hear both accounts. It would negotiate a present-day game-night charter, give the performers a stage, and hopefully finish before Shawna decided my private peace process had missed its final appointment. The old invoice was in a folder. The new invoice was considerably larger. My niggas, history had learned how to charge interest.
Who Is in Which Delegation? Whoever Says So.

Rae is a Black stud lesbian and a bike mechanic who likes detective stories, excellent snacks and a signing table that stands up. Kit is a butch lesbian and librarian with serious opinions about karaoke and no reliable idea where she left her glasses. Their rivalry concerns this particular evening, not a rule about what either label means.

Nia is a Black trans lesbian, a lawyer with terrible handwriting, and a woman who wants a dance with Rae. She belongs to more than one caucus. Mika is a trans nonbinary event planner with a miniature-hotel collection and a suspicious weakness for spectacular staging. They will sometimes improve the plan by making it considerably more expensive.

Velvet Payroll is a Black drag queen who wants a paid show and a properly lit stage. She uses she/her in these scenes. Remy is a trans man and drag king, performing as King Receipts, whose awful puns have survived every soundcheck. Drag describes what they perform; it does not turn the cast into a single gender or orientation.

The veterans are Auntie June, a Black butch lesbian and retired bus driver, and Odessa "Dez," a Black stud lesbian and retired seamstress. Both are fictional. Their 1967 feud is remembered with affection, unreliable detail and an unreasonable interest in who still owns one jacket.

Aiden narrates and pays. Shawna is his wife and has plans of her own. Tank, Rosa, Mercedes, Porsche, Dre and Darnell bring the established Tellings party energy. All the people in these invented scenes are adults. Lillian remains the reader. The new summit cast and relationships belong to this generated companion, not to a claim about the source novels or real people.

The fictional crew's printed chorus is deliberately excessive: fifteen uses of the reclaimed plural on every fixed PDF page, including covers and indexes. It occupies a separate band. EPUB pages change with the reader's font and screen, so the reflowable edition carries the chorus at chapter boundaries instead. The practical cards remain ordinary readable descriptions.
The Game Card Comes Before the Summit

Pick a genre or a title. Read the short pitch, what you actually do, the main catch and a first try. The longer explanation follows if you want it. The fiction comes afterward. You can understand why a game sounds interesting without reading a treaty, knowing the cast or doing any arithmetic.

The three labels describe editorial fit: A place to start is a promising candidate; Read the catch first identifies an obstacle to check; A more demanding detour is a narrower or harder possibility. The collection includes different levels of complexity. None of these labels describes the reader's intelligence or determines what they can enjoy.

The exact edition matters. An old adventure and its modern remake can ask for different movement, camera and inventory actions. Two people discussing one single-player mystery is different from a game with native co-op. The source notes keep these distinctions visible and leave unsupported features unknown.

The elaborate route is optional. A refusal costs nothing. You can stop, change games, ask for a reminder or prefer conversation. A first try is one meaningful action, not a prescribed duration or a test with a passing grade. This is leisure, not treatment.

The new coalition has no authority over your evening. "Then what are we signing?" I asked. Nia handed me the venue bill. "Your part is very clear." Shawna pulled out the chair beside her. The useful part of the evening was already happening there.
rules: Article 1. Enter through any door you like

Choose a department by what you want to do. Book I investigates suspicious people. Book II lets a turn wait for you. Book III looks around. Book IV moves ideas and objects into place. Book V listens to characters. Book VI brings company. A game belongs to one shelf in this Panorama so the count stays honest; its pleasures can overlap several shelves.
For the practical route, choose two titles from a shelf, read the catch, and try the more appealing opening. For the ceremonial route, continue below. The ceremony does not know better than you do.

Kit said the mystery room needed a better name. Rae suggested "the room with the mysteries." Velvet proposed "Evidence, Darling." I offered "The Aiden Memorial Institute of Suspicion." "You're alive," Nia said. "And still talking," Rae added. Mika printed MYSTERIES on a sheet of paper and taped it to the door. The room became easier to find. My niggas had negotiated a sign by declining to negotiate with me.
Article 2. Name what the evening needs

Write or say up to three actual preferences: no required rush; no separate camera steering; avoid held input; few menus; light reading; little clue tracking; or native co-op. Add any theme you do not want. You can choose fewer than three or add your own.

These are boundaries for the selection, not traits assigned to a person. They can change next time. The record should read “tonight, no camera wrestling,” not an assessment of somebody’s capabilities. One is useful information. The other is a stranger wearing a clipboard.

A source gap is not permission to promise a feature. If we have not established how a game handles a requirement, its card is a question to check or a reason to choose another game. The optional web finder treats strict feature filters conservatively. The printed cards put the concrete catch beside the temptation.

Rae wanted no sudden rush and a place to put her drink. Kit wanted a story with somebody worth arguing about. Nia wanted to sit beside Rae. I began assigning each wish a ministry. "Nigga, hers needs a chair," Tank said. Nia pulled one over herself. The coalition resolved its first territorial question by moving furniture six inches.
Article 3. Choose a row, because the binder demands coordinates

Each department has forty cases. Pick one of five rows: 1, Quietly Curious; 2, Ready for a Conversation; 3, Willing to Inspect a Thing; 4, Here for the Atmosphere; 5, Open to a Wildcard. These are ceremonial mood names. They do not certify that every game on a row meets that mood; the actual card and preferences decide that.

Choose a row freely. If you want dice, roll one ordinary six-sided die. Results 1–5 select that row. On a 6, visit the Incident Desk once and then choose a row yourself. There is no recursive reroll trap. The Incident Desk has had its authority to extend the evening revoked.

I called the mood rows a psychological instrument. Mika asked who had calibrated it. I said I liked the typeface. Velvet selected Here for the Atmosphere while adjusting an earring large enough to alter it. "My niggas, an instrument," Tank said, "is what Mercedes is trying to play while you explain the fucking menu." I left the mood rows to their modest work.
Article 4. Select the object whose paperwork you distrust

Choose an emblem, or roll an eight-sided die: 1 Envelope, 2 Key, 3 Plant, 4 Map, 5 Teacup, 6 Spare Chair, 7 Gold Stamp, 8 Clock. Read the corresponding column of the department’s five-by-eight route grid.

The grid gives a case number. For example, department 1, row 2, emblem 3 gives local case 11, P011. Department 6 at those same coordinates gives P211. The same coordinates in different departments lead to different games. This is either a filing system or a multiverse, depending on whether you are speaking to Shawna or me.

Remy chose the Gold Stamp because it matched his jacket. Kit chose the Key because hers were missing. Rae selected the Spare Chair and immediately sat in it. I tried to explain that it was symbolic. "Then symbolically get another one," she said. Nia moved her bag. We had a perfectly good emblem and an actual seat, and I was the only person dissatisfied.
Article 5. Optional: give the evening an outrageously specific title

Write one short session trait. Examples: “Two Detectives, One Sandwich”; “The Map Can Come to Me”; “I Want to Know What She Meant by That”; “A House with Excellent Stopping Places”; “The Plant Is Lying”; “My Friend Has the Other Controller.” A trait describes a taste or a situation, not a diagnosis.

Whenever it helps explain why a title sounds interesting, point to it. That explanation is already useful. You do not need a numeric bonus to care about a haunted town or a witness with a suspicious alibi.

If you enjoy the machinery, begin with three imaginary Stamp Tokens. Spend one to add two to the paperwork total OR reroll all four paperwork dice once. At most one token per selection. Refusing costs nothing; tokens never buy exceptions to preferences.

Velvet named her trait Paid Before the Encore. Remy chose Entrance Music Longer Than the Entrance. I wrote Historically Indispensable Host. Shawna put a line through indispensable. "Keep the rest," she said. "You did book the room." My niggas had discovered the cheapest possible way to reduce a national monument.
Article 6. Four dice that cannot be cashed at the bar

Roll four ordinary six-sided dice. Each 1 or 2 means minus one, each 3 or 4 means zero, and each 5 or 6 means plus one. Add the four values. Your paperwork total is between minus four and plus four. This optional layer draws on Fate’s familiar signed-dice idea; the surrounding selection rules are original Panorama rules.

If you spend a Stamp Token, either add two or reroll all four dice once and use the new total. You cannot buy a second modification on this selection. Reset to three tokens whenever you begin a new browsing session; no ledger needs to survive dinner.
The dice can produce a total from minus four to plus four. A +2 stamp can raise that part to plus six; the separate refreshment adjustment can add another zero, one or two.

Kit rolled and began calculating. Rae watched her pencil. "You always look this serious?" "Only when somebody's pretending numbers are fate." Nia smiled into her glass. Velvet asked whether a plus two could extend her set. Mika said the arithmetic selected a game. "Fine. My contract selects the encore." Two systems, both suddenly clearer than mine.
Article 7. Optional: the snack amendment

Record a separate snack adjustment: one if somebody has already brought the drink they wanted, plus one if wanted snacks are within reach and no one is expected to fetch them. The maximum snack adjustment is two. Keep it separate from the dice-and-stamp paperwork total; Article 8 adds it exactly once. If these conditions are irrelevant, use zero. This arithmetic is a joke about hospitality; nobody needs to eat or drink anything to participate.
Do not delay choosing a game to qualify for this amendment. Do not make a snack score into a task for somebody else. The best possible snack state is people having what they actually want.

Rae negotiated for better crisps. Kit supported her motion immediately, which spoiled my photograph of historic rivalry. Dre set down the casserole and Tank became the first delegate to support the amendment with both hands. "My niggas," I said, "let the record show—" Rosa gave me a plate. For once the record benefited from silence.
Article 8. The entirely unnecessary formula

First find the local case from the grid: eight times (row minus one), plus emblem. Add the paperwork total and the snack adjustment, if you used them. If the result exceeds forty, subtract forty until it is 1–40. If it is below one, add forty until it is 1–40. Otherwise keep it. The final local case number is always between 1 and 40.

Then add forty times (department minus one) to get the complete P-number. Department 3, row 1, emblem 2 starts at local case 2. A paperwork total of minus three and a snack adjustment of one gives zero. Wrap zero to forty. In department 3, local case forty is P120.

This is a shelf address. It is not a probability of enjoyment, a cognitive score, a ranking, or an instruction to buy something. It chooses a page to consider. Read that page’s ordinary fields before treating it as a candidate.
If arithmetic gets in the way, use the offline finder or choose directly.

Mika checked the formula. Nia checked the example. Rae checked whether Kit was using the back of the menu as scrap paper. I asked who was checking the atmosphere. Velvet looked over her shoulder. "I invoiced you for that, darling." The shelf address survived the inspection. My claim to be essential did not.
Article 9. Read the game first; Aiden can wait

Read the short pitch, what you do, main catch and first try before the longer comic scene. The full appeal and catch give the detail behind those summaries. Aiden’s scene and verdict are fiction; a funny reason is not evidence for a game feature.

Check the exact edition and platform. A remake can change movement, menus and saves. A touch port can differ from a desktop pointer. A Steam store date may be the port’s date rather than the original release. Local co-op, online co-op and two people discussing a single-player game are not interchangeable.

If the card conflicts with a real preference, reject the candidate. If it is promising but has an unresolved operation, check that specific operation before investing in it. “Can we select this inventory object comfortably?” is more useful than “Is this an easy game?”

The screen showed a beautiful landscape. I declared it perfect for everybody. Kit asked about the camera. Rae asked about holding buttons. Nia asked which edition I was looking at. "My niggas," Tank said, "you can't answer a control question with a sunset." I turned the card over and read the part I should have read first.
Article 10. The appeals court

You may make one ceremonial appeal or skip the ceremony entirely. To appeal, choose a neighbor: the previous local case, the next local case, or the same local case in another department. Wrap case 1 backward to 40 and case 40 forward to 1. Check the new card as usual.

After that one appeal, stop calculating. Choose either candidate, browse the direct index or close the book. Every route ends with a human decision; there is no compulsory loop, escalating fee or penalty for declining both.
If you would rather talk, talk. If you would rather stop, stop.

I appealed the seating chart because I was no longer in the middle. Nia asked whether I wanted to be near Shawna or near the photographer. I said both. Shawna held out her hand. The photographer moved to the buffet. My niggas, a constitutional crisis ended with one entirely reasonable choice, and I did not require a second hearing.
Article 11. A genuinely useful first session

Load the chosen edition before introducing its controls. Show one meaningful action. Keep a reminder if wanted. Find pause, save or exit so leaving feels ordinary. Do not turn a trial into a lesson with a hidden passing grade.

For a mystery, that might mean one conversation or one clue. For an exploration game, a nearby path and a place to stop. For a turn-based game, one decision with the menus already explained. For co-op, agree who wants which role and whether the roles have equal kinds of action.

Stop, change games or take a break whenever wanted. A day off makes room for leisure; it does not require a whole day of screen time. The useful note afterward is a sentence about what was enjoyable and where to resume.

Rae tried one clue. Kit had a theory. Nia listened and then offered a different one. Nobody asked me to introduce the game. I stood there with the microphone until Mika took it gently out of my hand. "There," they said. "Your first useful action." I went to find Shawna, who had saved me a seat without establishing a department for it.
Article 12. What these departments are allowed to claim

This is a researched, source-linked candidate catalogue with original comic writing. Game descriptions were checked against publisher, developer, platform or identified supporting sources. Control classifications and first-trial suggestions are editorial judgments unless tied to an explicit declaration. No card claims a complete-path playtest.

The catalogue deliberately contains different levels of complexity. Turn-based strategy and elaborate deduction belong here only for readers who want those specific demands. The direct index and catches let you pass them by. “There are two hundred and forty games” does not mean “all two hundred and forty will suit the same evening.”

The offline finder uses the same case IDs as the books. It makes no network requests and does not inspect your library. Marking a title interesting does not install or buy it. Its strict feature filters require stated evidence; an unknown is not silently accepted.

I announced that the catalogue proved universal happiness was possible. Velvet asked whether I had tried every game. "Not personally." "Then put that on the same fucking poster." Nia uncapped the thick pen. My niggas, an honest limitation arrived with better handwriting than my slogan, which was impressive because Nia's handwriting was terrible.
incidents: The rival lecterns form a table
Rae and Kit cooperate before Aiden can photograph the rivalry. Choose a row; repairing the furniture does not change a game feature.
Three badges, one delegate
Nia sits with both caucuses. Aiden orders another badge and receives another bill. Choose a row; no identity adds or subtracts points.
The drag programme has a rider
Velvet finds an unpaid rehearsal in the schedule. Mika finds a pen. Choose a row while the performance gets its own agreement.
King Receipts enters twice
Remy wants the cash-register fanfare to land properly. The second entrance is worse and he enjoys it more. Choose a row; no encore roll.
The cocaine is not a centrepiece
Darnell misunderstands the hospitality plan. Rosa clears the game table and Dre puts down dinner. Choose a row; no fictional drug affects the route.
The karaoke caucus expands
Kit starts a song and discovers Rae knows the harmony. Aiden loses his scheduled welcome slot. Choose a row.
The trans delegation has the actual key
Mika opens the side room everyone has been debating. It contains chairs. Choose a row; you do not have to hold a meeting to sit down.
A dance enters the minutes
Nia asks Rae directly. Rae says yes. Aiden tries to record a historic development and is told to find his own wife. Choose a row.
The blue controller has no foreign policy
Dre calls dibs, then offers to swap when somebody wants that seat. Aiden abandons his theory about international colours. Choose a row.
The treaty pen is a eyeliner pencil
Velvet retrieves her property. Kit lends an ordinary pen. Choose a row while the summit discovers affordable stationery.
Private negotiations upstairs
Shawna and Aiden leave their own agenda out of the public record. Tank can say choose a row without a ceremonial sash. Choose one whenever wanted.
The portrait receives no reimbursement
All caucuses agree the giant picture of Aiden was his own decision. Choose a row; unanimity is occasionally very inexpensive.

Prefer a desk, static scene or fixed framing; check the actual movement and camera.

Nia Came for the Story and Stayed for Rae
Character interest can motivate a game; reading load and choice pressure remain separate questions.

Explore because the place interests you; test movement and looking around before a longer journey.
